title: Nutrient supply ratios and size‐structured competition regulate global diatom ecology and biogeochemistry
content:
Abstract

Diatoms are major contributors to oceanic photosynthesis and global biogeochemical cycling, particularly through their role in the silicon cycle. Previous theories have emphasized the importance of silicon-to-nitrogen (Si : N) ratios in regulating diatom ecology. Here we extend this framework to include the role of iron (Fe) limitation, phytoplankton size structure, and density-dependent losses. We develop a theoretical resource-competition model in which picophytoplankton, nanophytoplankton, and diatoms compete for nitrate, silicate, and iron under defined ecophysiological trade-offs. The model predicts that the absolute supply of N and Fe regulates the relative success of small and large phytoplankton, while the supply of Si relative to N or Fe determines the relative success of diatoms within the larger fraction. In general, the relative supply ratios of Si : N : Fe define four distinct biogeochemical provinces, each characterized by different limiting nutrients, community composition, and surface nutrient concentrations. These predictions are tested using a global ocean ecosystem model with multiple plankton functional types and size classes. The global model reproduces the provinces predicted by theory and captures large-scale patterns in surface nutrients and diatom biomass. The revised theoretical framework explains why Si : N supply ratios alone are poor predictors of global diatom biogeography and why Si : Fe supply ratios provide a stronger indicator of elevated diatom biomass fractions. These findings suggest that nutrient supply ratios, absolute nutrient supply, and size-structured top-down control together regulate the ecological and biogeochemical function of diatoms in the ocean.
